quiz.question: What is the difference between Git, GitHub, a commit, a branch, a tag and a release?
options: Git is a local version control system; GitHub is a hosting platform; a commit is an immutable snapshot; a branch is a movable reference to a commit; a tag is a static named reference; a release is a published software version with notes/artifacts.
Git is a cloud platform; GitHub is a terminal command; a commit is a branch; a tag is a working tree.
They are all interchangeable synonyms in modern CI/CD.
Git and GitHub are identical open-source software tools run on Linux servers.

quiz.question: What do the working directory, staging area (index) and local repository represent?
options: Working directory: uncommitted local files; Staging area: binary cache of files selected for the next commit snapshot; Local repository: committed permanent history stored in .git.
Working directory: cloud storage; Staging area: RAM cache; Local repository: GitHub server.
They are all identical directories inside the user's home folder.
Staging area is only used when internet connection fails.

quiz.question: Why should commits represent small, logically coherent changes rather than giant unrelated updates?
options: Because Git has a hard file size limit of 10KB per commit.
Coherent commits make code review manageable, allow precise regression tracking via git bisect, and enable clean rollbacks via git revert without unintended side effects.
To artificially inflate developer contribution metrics on GitHub profiles.
Because merge conflicts cannot occur if commits are small.

quiz.question: What is the difference between merging and rebasing, and why should shared history be treated carefully?
options: Merging creates a 3-way merge commit preserving exact history topology; rebasing replays commits onto a new base creating linear history by rewriting commit hashes. Rewriting shared history breaks collaborators' local branch ancestry.
Merging deletes files while rebasing compresses them.
Rebase can only be used on GitHub's website; merge is only run in the terminal.
Rebasing preserves commit hashes; merging generates new hashes.

quiz.question: What causes a merge conflict, and how can an SRE verify its resolution before completing the merge?
options: A conflict occurs when two branches edit the exact same lines of a file or modify/delete the same file. Verification requires removing all conflict markers, running test suites/linters, and inspecting git diff --staged.
Conflicts are caused by server network timeouts during git push.
Conflicts only happen if .gitignore is missing.
A conflict is automatically resolved by Git deleting the older file.

quiz.question: What does a Pull Request (PR) add beyond a raw 'git push'?
options: It provides a structured collaboration framework: visual diff inspection, peer code reviews, CI/CD automated test gates, discussion threads, and policy enforcement via branch protection rules.
It speeds up internet bandwidth for large git pushes.
It converts bash scripts into compiled C binaries automatically.
It is merely a notification email with no extra tools.

quiz.question: What should a professional code reviewer examine beyond simple syntax errors?
options: Correctness, system design/architecture, unnecessary complexity, readability/maintainability, security risks (permissions/secrets), operational safety (logging/error handling), and backward compatibility.
Only code indentation, semicolons, and variable naming aesthetics.
Whether the author used spaces or tabs exclusively.
Reviewers should only verify whether the CI build passed.

quiz.question: How can you undo a shared commit in production without rewriting its history?
options: Use 'git revert <commit-hash>', which creates a new forward commit that applies the inverse diff of the faulty change.
Run 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' and 'git push --force'.
Delete the repository on GitHub and re-push from a backup USB drive.
Edit the file manually and leave commit history unchanged.

quiz.question: Why is adding an accidentally committed secret to .gitignore insufficient?
options: .gitignore only prevents untracked files from being staged in the future; it does NOT remove files already stored in the Git commit object database.
Because .gitignore is ignored by GitHub.
Because .gitignore files can be read by anyone on the internet.
Because secrets in .gitignore cause the Git compiler to crash.

quiz.question: Under Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, when should a project increment MAJOR, MINOR, or PATCH?
options: MAJOR: Incompatible/breaking API or CLI changes; MINOR: Backward-compatible new functionality; PATCH: Backward-compatible bug fixes.
MAJOR: Yearly; MINOR: Monthly; PATCH: Daily.
MAJOR: When UI changes color; MINOR: When a developer is promoted; PATCH: On weekends.

Tags do not reference commits; they reference GitHub issues.

topics.title: Understand Git Before Memorizing Commands
topics.summary: Why ad-hoc scripts like 'script-final-v2.sh' fail. Git is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of immutable snapshots, not differential patch files. The 4 primary areas: Working Tree, Index (Staging), Local Repository, and Remote Repository.

details.heading: The Anti-Pattern of Manual Versioning
details.body: Without version control, engineers fall into the trap of 'script-final.sh', 'script-final-new.sh', 'script-final-working.sh'. In production, this makes it impossible to answer: Which version worked last Tuesday? Who modified the disk health check? Why was an authorization check removed? Can we instantly roll back a broken deploy? Git answers these by recording immutable, cryptographically hashed snapshots linked in a causal graph.

details.heading: Git History is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
details.body: Unlike older VCS tools (CVS/SVN) that stored file diffs (deltas), Git stores a sequence of snapshots. Each commit contains metadata (author, timestamp, commit message) and a cryptographic tree pointer representing the exact directory state. Crucially, each commit points backward to its parent commit(s). Branches in Git are not heavy copies of your project; a branch is merely a lightweight, 41-byte movable pointer referencing a commit SHA.

details.heading: The Four Areas of Everyday Git
details.body:
Every command navigates across 4 distinct zones:
1. Working Directory: The actual sandbox files on your filesystem currently being edited.
2. Staging Area (Index): The binary cache (`.git/index`) representing the exact snapshot prepared for the next commit.
3. Local Repository: The permanent local history of committed snapshots stored in `.git/objects`.
4. Remote Repository: The shared remote repository hosted on GitHub/GitLab used for team synchronization.

details.heading: Git vs. GitHub: Foundational Separation
details.body: Git is a local-first distributed version control system developed by Linus Torvalds in 2005. It functions entirely offline on your workstation. GitHub is a hosted cloud platform that wraps Git repositories with collaborative engineering tools: Pull Requests, code review discussions, issue trackers, CI/CD Actions, and enterprise access permissions.

topics.codeSnippet:
# Visualizing the 4 zones of Git
# 1. Inspect working tree vs index (staging)
git status

# 2. Add specific files to index (prepare snapshot)
git add linux-admin.sh

# 3. Commit staged snapshot to local repository
git commit -m "feat(diagnostics): add inode exhaustion check"

# 4. Push local commits to remote GitHub repository
git push origin main

topics.title: Install, Configure & Secure Identity
topics.summary: Global vs repository configuration. Author identity vs committer identity. Inspecting configuration origins. Eliminating hardcoded secrets from git configuration files.

details.heading: Package Installation Across Linux Distributions
details.body:
On modern Debian/Ubuntu servers:
`sudo apt update && sudo apt install git -y`
On RHEL/CentOS/Rocky Linux:
`sudo dnf install git -y`
Verify installation using `git --version` (Git 2.34+ recommended for modern `switch`/`restore` primitives).

details.heading: Configuring Commit Identity
details.body:
Git commits embed author and committer names and email addresses. Configure these globally for your user environment:
`git config --global user.name "Jane Doe"`
`git config --global user.email "jane.doe@company.internal"`
GitHub also provides a privacy no-reply email (e.g., `ID+username@users.noreply.github.com`) to prevent public scraping of corporate emails.

details.heading: Configuration Hierarchy & Inspection
details.body:
Git evaluates configuration in three cascading tiers:
1. System level (`/etc/gitconfig`): Applies to all OS users.
2. Global level (`~/.gitconfig`): Applies to your current OS user account.
3. Local level (`.git/config`): Repository-specific overrides.
Inspect all active keys and their file origins with:
`git config --list --show-origin`

details.heading: Security Rule: No Credentials in Configuration
details.body: Never store plaintext passwords, personal access tokens (PATs), or private keys in Git configuration files. Use SSH keys registered with `ssh-agent`, or modern Git Credential Managers that store authentication tokens in secure OS keyrings (libsecret on Linux, Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows).

topics.codeSnippet:
# Verify Git version
git --version

# Set global identity
git config --global user.name "SRE Engineer"
git config --global user.email "sre@infrastructure.io"

# Set default primary branch to 'main'
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Inspect all configurations and origins
git config --list --show-origin

topics.title: Repository Initialization, Commits & .gitignore
topics.summary: Initializing projects with 'git init -b main'. Atomic commits and Conventional Commits format. The critical purpose of .gitignore and why it cannot remediate committed secrets.

details.heading: Project Initialization
details.body:
Initialize your DevOps infrastructure repository with modern default branch naming:
`mkdir linux-admin-toolkit && cd linux-admin-toolkit`
`git init -b main`
This creates the hidden `.git` directory containing object databases, refs, and the index.

details.heading: Atomic, Coherent Commits
details.body: A commit should be atomic: a single, logically coherent unit of work that leaves the system in a compiling, testable state. Avoid the anti-pattern of 'giant Friday commit' containing 50 unrelated edits across documentation, backend logic, and config files. When changes are atomic, bugs can be easily isolated with `git bisect` and cleanly rolled back with `git revert`.

details.heading: The Conventional Commits Standard
details.body:
Adopt semantic commit prefixes to enable automated changelogs and clear history:
- `feat:` Introduces new functionality.
- `fix:` Patches a bug or operational defect.
- `docs:` Modifies documentation or runbooks.
- `test:` Adds or modifies unit/integration test suites.
- `refactor:` Code restructuring without functional behavior changes.
- `chore:` Maintenance tasks, dependency updates, tooling.

details.heading: Staging Inspection Workflow
details.body:
Never blind commit (`git commit -a`). Always execute the two-phase diff inspection:
1. `git diff`: Shows changes in the working tree not yet staged.
2. `git diff --staged`: Shows the exact diff that will be committed to the repository.
This inspection catches debugging print statements, temporary files, and accidental secrets before they reach the repository.

details.heading: .gitignore Hygiene & The Secret Committal Danger
details.body:
A `.gitignore` file specifies intentionally untracked patterns (e.g., `.env`, `*.log`, `__pycache__/`, `.venv/`).
CRITICAL WARNING: `.gitignore` only prevents untracked files from being added. If a developer accidentally commits a secret (like an AWS secret or database password) and then adds `.env` to `.gitignore` in a subsequent commit, the secret REMAINS PERMANENTLY ACCESSIBLE in repository history!

topics.codeSnippet:
# Initialize repo with main branch
git init -b main

# Inspect staging area
git status
git diff          # unstaged changes
git diff --staged # staged changes ready to commit

# Commit with Conventional Commit message
git commit -m "feat(storage): implement inode exhaustion threshold warning"

# View oneline decorated graph history
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

topics.title: Branches & Collaborative Development
topics.summary: Branches as lightweight 41-byte pointers. Modern 'git switch -c' vs legacy checkout. Branch naming conventions. Implementing GitHub Flow in SRE teams.

details.heading: How Git Branches Actually Work
details.body: In Git, a branch is not a directory copy or heavy container. It is literally a 41-byte text file inside `.git/refs/heads/<branch-name>` containing the 40-character SHA hash of the commit it points to. Because creating a branch merely writes a 41-byte text file, branching is instantaneous and virtually free in storage overhead.

details.heading: Modern Branch Switching: git switch
details.body:
Historically, `git checkout` was overloaded with two unrelated duties: switching branches and discarding working file modifications. Git 2.23+ introduced dedicated commands:
- `git switch -c feature/resource-report`: Creates and switches to a new branch.
- `git switch main`: Returns to the main branch.
- `git restore <file>`: Discards unstaged file edits safely.

details.heading: SRE Branch Naming Conventions
details.body:
Establish consistent, hierarchical branch names across the team:
- `feature/disk-health-json`: New telemetry capabilities.
- `fix/nginx-socket-leak`: Defect remediation.
- `ops/rotate-tls-certs`: Infrastructure maintenance.
- `docs/troubleshooting-runbook`: SRE incident documentation.

details.heading: GitHub Flow Collaboration Model
details.body:
GitHub Flow is a lightweight, battle-tested branching model:
1. Anything in the `main` branch is production-ready and deployable.
2. To work on something new, create a descriptive branch off `main`.
3. Commit small, logical changes locally and regularly push to the remote.
4. Open a Pull Request targeting `main` to solicit review and run automated tests.
5. Once approved and CI checks pass, merge into `main` and deploy immediately.

topics.codeSnippet:
# Create and switch to a feature branch
git switch -c feature/systemd-service-check

# Make edits and commit to the branch
git add linux-admin.sh
git commit -m "feat(services): verify systemd unit active states"

# View local and remote tracking branches
git branch -avv

# Switch back to primary branch
git switch main

topics.title: Merge vs. Rebase: Architectural Trade-offs
topics.summary: 3-way merges vs linear rebasing. When to use each. The Golden Rule of Rebasing: Never rebase or force-push a public/shared branch.

details.heading: The Merge Strategy: Context-Preserving Integration
details.body: When you run `git merge feature/diagnostics` on `main`, Git performs a 3-way merge using the two branch tips and their common ancestor. If histories have diverged, Git generates a merge commit with two parent commits. Advantage: completely preserves historical context and exact timestamps without rewriting history. Disadvantage: can create tangled 'railroad track' graph histories in high-frequency teams.

details.heading: The Rebase Strategy: Linear Replaying
details.body: Rebase replays your branch commits on top of the target branch (`origin/main`). Git sequentially extracts the diff of each commit on your branch and applies it as a brand-new commit (with a brand-new commit SHA) on the tip of the upstream branch. Advantage: produces a clean, perfectly linear commit history. Disadvantage: rewrites commit timestamps and hashes.

details.heading: The SRE Golden Rule of Rebasing
details.body: CRITICAL SAFETY DOCTRINE: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a public or shared remote repository! Rebasing rewrites commit IDs ($C_1 \rightarrow C_1'$). If other team members branched off your original commit, their histories diverge catastrophically, forcing painful manual reconciliations.

details.heading: The Danger of git push --force
details.body: Routine use of `git push --force` (`-f`) is an operational hazard that can overwrite colleagues' work. If a private feature branch history rewrite must be published, always use `git push --force-with-lease`. This flags and rejects the push if someone else pushed commits to the remote branch since your last fetch.

topics.codeSnippet:
# Method 1: Merging (Preserves history & merge commit)
git switch main
git merge feature/resource-report

# Method 2: Rebasing (Creates linear history on private branch)
git switch feature/resource-report
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# Safe force-push for private rebased feature branches
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/resource-report

topics.title: Merge Conflicts: Mechanics & Resolution
topics.summary: Why conflicts happen. Deconstructing conflict markers (HEAD vs incoming). Systematic resolution workflow and safe rollback via 'git merge --abort'.

details.heading: Anatomy of a Merge Conflict
details.body: A conflict occurs when Git cannot deterministically reconcile changes because two branches modified the exact same lines of a file since their common ancestor, or one branch deleted a file that the other modified. Git pauses execution, enters a merging state, and inserts visual conflict markers directly into the affected files.

details.heading: Deconstructing Conflict Markers
details.body:
A conflict block consists of three sections:
`<<<<<<< HEAD`: Marks the start of changes on your current branch (e.g., `main`).
`=======`: The middle delimiter separating competing modifications.
`>>>>>>> branch-name`: The incoming changes from the branch being integrated.
These markers are not valid code syntax and must be completely removed during resolution.

details.heading: Systematic 4-Step Resolution Workflow
details.body:
1. Identify: Run `git status` to locate files listed under 'Unmerged paths'.
2. Reconcile: Open each file, analyze the intent of both changes, edit the code into the intended unified state, and delete all `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers.
3. Validate: Run unit tests, linters, or syntax validators to ensure the merged file functions properly.
4. Finalize: Run `git add <file>` to mark resolved, then execute `git merge --continue` (or `git commit`) to finalize the merge.

details.heading: The Escape Hatch: git merge --abort
details.body: If a conflict is too complex or was started by mistake, never attempt manual guesswork. Run `git merge --abort`. This cleanly rolls back your working tree and index to the exact state before the merge was initiated.

topics.codeSnippet:
# 1. Check which files are in conflict
git status

# 2. After editing and removing conflict markers:
git add linux-admin.sh

# 3. Complete the merge
git merge --continue

# Emergency Escape Hatch: Cancel merge and restore previous state
git merge --abort

topics.title: GitHub Remotes & The Pull Request Lifecycle
topics.summary: Connecting remotes with 'git remote add origin'. Upstream tracking flags (-u). The 8-stage PR lifecycle and enterprise branch protection rules.

details.heading: Connecting Local Repositories to Remotes
details.body:
A remote is a reference to a hosted repository on GitHub. Connect an existing local repository:
`git remote add origin https://github.com/organization/linux-admin-toolkit.git`
Verify configured remote URLs:
`git remote -v`
The `-u` (or `--set-upstream`) flag during `git push -u origin main` binds your local `main` branch to the remote `origin/main` tracking branch, allowing subsequent simple `git push` and `git pull` commands.

details.heading: The 8-Stage Pull Request Lifecycle
details.body:
A Pull Request (PR) is a formal mechanism to propose, discuss, review, and test changes before merging:
1. Create focused feature branch from latest `main`.
2. Commit atomic, well-tested changes.
3. Push branch to remote.
4. Open Pull Request on GitHub with a comprehensive description.
5. Automated CI pipelines execute (linters, unit tests, security scans).
6. Team peer review and discussions.
7. Address review feedback with iterative commits.
8. Merge approved PR into `main` and delete the feature branch.

details.heading: Structuring an Elite PR Description
details.body:
A professional PR description answers 4 questions for the reviewer:
- Context/Problem: Why is this change necessary? (Link Jira/GitHub issue).
- Proposed Solution: How does this change solve the issue?
- Validation & Testing: What tests, commands, or edge cases were verified?
- Operational Impact: Does this require downtime, migration, or permission changes?

details.heading: Enterprise Branch Protection Rules
details.body:
To maintain production stability, GitHub repositories should enforce branch protection on `main`:
- Require pull request reviews before merging (e.g., minimum 1 senior SRE approval).
- Require status checks to pass before merging (CI test matrix, ShellCheck, security scanner).
- Require conversation resolution before merging.
- Prohibit force pushes and branch deletions on `main`.

topics.codeSnippet:
# Add GitHub remote
git remote add origin https://github.com/corp/linux-admin-toolkit.git
git remote -v

# Push branch and set upstream tracking
git push -u origin feature/service-diagnostics

# Fetch remote updates without auto-merging
git fetch origin

# Fast-forward pull with rebase
git pull --rebase origin main

topics.title: Google-Grade Code Review Doctrine for SREs
topics.summary: Code review as a quality and knowledge-sharing engine. Google's 8 review dimensions. Operational reviews for bash & infrastructure automation. High-empathy actionable comments.

details.heading: The Purpose of Code Review
details.body: Following Google Engineering Practices (`eng-practices`), code review is not an adversarial gatekeeping exercise or a race to find minor formatting flaws. Its purpose is to maintain and improve code health, ensure architectural alignment, prevent operational defects, and mentor team members.

details.heading: The SRE Review Dimension Matrix
details.body:
A production infrastructure reviewer evaluates changes across 8 critical dimensions:
1. Correctness: Does the code actually perform what it claims without edge-case regressions?
2. Design: Does it fit into the broader system architecture cleanly?
3. Complexity: Is the code unnecessarily complicated? Can it be simplified?
4. Readability: Will an on-call engineer at 3:00 AM understand this script during an outage?
5. Security: Does it expose credentials, rely on untrusted input, or require excessive `sudo` privileges?
6. Operations: Does it log meaningful error messages with timestamps, or fail silently?
7. Testing: Are failure scenarios and non-zero exit codes tested?
8. Backward Compatibility: Will this break existing cron jobs, APIs, or downstream scripts?

details.heading: Constructive vs Destructive Review Comments
details.body:
Weak/Unhelpful: 'This is bad. Rewrite it.'
Constructive/Actionable: 'This while-loop restarts Nginx every second without a backoff timer. If Nginx crashes due to a corrupt configuration, this will flood the journal logs and max CPU. Could we use systemd's built-in Restart=always directive with a RestartSec=5s delay instead?'

details.heading: Distinguishing Blockers from Nits
details.body:
Reviewers must explicitly categorize comments:
- Blocker: Correctness, security vulnerability, or production failure risk (must be resolved before merge).
- `nit:` (Optional suggestion): Stylistic or minor preference that does not block merging.

topics.codeSnippet:
# Example SRE review comment template:
# [Category]: Blocker | Security | Operations | Nit
# [Observation]: What specific line or pattern introduces risk
# [Impact]: How this manifests under production failure conditions
# [Recommendation]: Specific code replacement or architectural alternative

topics.title: Tags, Releases & Semantic Versioning (SemVer)
topics.summary: Annotated tags vs lightweight tags. GitHub Releases vs Git Tags. Semantic Versioning rules: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. The immutability of released versions.

details.heading: Lightweight vs. Annotated Tags
details.body:
A lightweight tag is just a pointer to a commit (like a branch that doesn't move).
An annotated tag is stored as a full object in the Git database. It contains tagger name, email, date, GPG signature, and a release message. Releases should ALWAYS use annotated tags:
`git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0: Initial production release"`
Push specific tags using `git push origin v1.0.0`.

details.heading: Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0) Specification
details.body:
Software versions follow the format: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (e.g., `2.4.1`):
1. MAJOR (X.0.0): Incremented when incompatible API or CLI breaking changes are introduced.
2. MINOR (1.X.0): Incremented when functionality is added in a backward-compatible manner.
3. PATCH (1.0.X): Incremented when backward-compatible bug fixes or security patches are made.

details.heading: Applied SemVer in Infrastructure Automation
details.body:
For our `linux-admin.sh` toolkit:
- Bug fix: Fixing an awk column parsing bug without altering command syntax $\rightarrow$ `1.0.1` (PATCH).
- New Feature: Adding `--json` output flag while keeping text output default $\rightarrow$ `1.1.0` (MINOR).
- Breaking Change: Renaming `--check-disk` to `-d` and removing the long flag $\rightarrow$ `2.0.0` (MAJOR).

details.heading: The Release Immutability Rule
details.body: Once a version tag (e.g., `v1.2.0`) is published and packaged into a release, it must be treated as immutable. Never delete and retag a published version to slip in a bug fix. If an error is discovered in `v1.2.0`, cut and publish `v1.2.1`.

topics.codeSnippet:
# Create annotated release tag
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0: Linux admin toolkit initial release"

# Inspect tag metadata and referenced commit
git show v1.0.0

# Push tag to GitHub remote
git push origin v1.0.0

# Push all local tags
git push origin --tags

topics.title: Disaster Recovery: SRE Playbook & Incident Protocol
topics.summary: Undoing mistakes with 'git restore', 'git revert', and 'git reflog'. SRE Emergency Protocol: What to do when a secret is committed to Git.

details.heading: Recovering from Working Tree & Staging Mistakes
details.body:
- Unstage a file without losing edits: `git restore --staged <file>`
- Discard unstaged working tree changes: `git restore <file>` (CAUTION: Destructive!)
- Amend the most recent commit: `git commit --amend` (Only for private, unpushed commits!).

details.heading: Undoing Shared Commits: git revert
details.body: If a bad commit was already pushed to `main` and shared across the team, NEVER use `git reset --hard`! That rewrites history and breaks downstream clones. Instead, run `git revert <commit-hash>`. This creates a brand new commit that performs the exact mathematical opposite diff of the faulty commit, cleanly reversing the change while preserving auditability.

details.heading: The SRE Time Machine: git reflog
details.body: Git records every change of HEAD in the reference log (`git reflog`). If an engineer runs `git reset --hard` and panics thinking their work was destroyed, `git reflog` shows the commit hashes before the reset. You can instantly recover the lost state with `git switch -c recovery-branch <commit-hash>`.

details.heading: Emergency Incident Protocol: Secret Committed to Git
details.body:
Scenario: An engineer committed an active AWS API key or production database password.
Protocol:
1. IMMEDIATE REVOCATION: Log in to AWS IAM or database console and rotate/revoke the credential immediately. Never assume the secret is safe.
2. AUDIT: Review AWS CloudTrail / audit logs for unauthorized access.
3. HISTORY SCRUB: Use `git-filter-repo` or BFG Repo-Cleaner to rewrite history and purge the secret from all commit trees.
4. FORCE PUSH SANITIZED REPO: Push sanitized branches and notify all team members to re-clone the repository.

topics.codeSnippet:
# 1. Undo staged file
git restore --staged linux-admin.sh

# 2. Safely reverse a shared commit in production
git revert 8b9c0d1 -m "revert: rollback buggy disk check"

# 3. View reference log to recover 'lost' commits
git reflog
# Recover lost state from reflog:
git switch -c rescue-branch HEAD@{2}

scenarios.prTitle: PR #14: Add automated remediation loop for dead services
scenarios.author: alex-dev (Junior DevOps Engineer)
scenarios.diffSnippet:
+ # Auto-restart loop
+ while true; do
+   if ! systemctl is-active --quiet nginx; then
+     echo "[ALERT] Nginx is down! Restarting immediately..."
+     systemctl restart nginx
+   fi
+   sleep 1
+ done
scenarios.riskSummary: Bash infinite loop restarting a failing service every 1 second without backoff or limits.
scenarios.question: As an SRE Senior Reviewer following Google Engineering practices, what is your review decision?

options.label: Approve and Merge: It keeps Nginx running at all times automatically.
options.explanation: Dangerous in production! If Nginx is crashing due to a bad config or port conflict, restarting it every second creates a CPU storm, masks the crash loop, and prevents maintenance downtime.

options.label: Request Changes: Keep script read-only by default, rely on systemd Restart=always with RestartSec=5s, or add rate-limiting/circuit breakers.
options.explanation: Correct! SRE review doctrine requires read-only defaults. Process supervision belongs in systemd unit files with exponential backoff, not ad-hoc unconstrained while-loops in bash scripts.

options.label: Approve with Nit: Ask to change sleep 1 to sleep 2.
options.explanation: Insufficient. A 2-second sleep does not fix the architectural flaw of bypassing systemd supervision.

scenarios.question: The author claims .gitignore now excludes .env and the secret is deleted. How should you respond?

options.label: Approve: The secret is deleted from the latest commit so it is no longer visible in the working tree.
options.explanation: Catastrophic misconception! Git preserves full immutable snapshot history. Anyone cloning the repo or inspecting 'git log -p' or commit 1 can read the cleartext AWS Secret Key.

options.label: Block PR & Trigger Security Incident: Immediately revoke/rotate the AWS IAM key, inspect AWS CloudTrail for unauthorized usage, and scrub git history via git-filter-repo.
options.explanation: Authoritative security doctrine: A secret once committed to git must be assumed compromised. Deleting it in a later commit is completely ineffective. Immediate revocation & rotation is mandatory.

options.label: Ask author to rebase and squash both commits into one.
options.explanation: While squashing cleans local history, if this branch was pushed to GitHub remote, the commit may already be cached, indexed, or cloned. Key revocation is always step #1.

scenarios.question: According to Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, what release tag must this change require if merged?

options.label: Increment PATCH (e.g., v1.0.1) because it is a simple syntax cleanup.
options.explanation: PATCH is strictly reserved for backward-compatible bug fixes that do not modify the public API.

options.label: Increment MINOR (e.g., v1.1.0) because new flags were added.
options.explanation: MINOR requires backward compatibility. If existing automated cron jobs calling '--check-disk' break, it is not backward compatible.

options.label: Increment MAJOR (e.g., v2.0.0) because removing documented flags breaks existing automation and consumers of the public CLI API.
options.explanation: Exact SemVer requirement: Removing or renaming documented public interfaces/flags is a breaking change requiring a MAJOR version increment (or maintaining deprecated alias flags).

scenarios.prTitle: PR #17: Force-pushed rebase on shared staging branch
scenarios.author: pat-ops (Infra Engineer)
scenarios.diffSnippet:
[remote rejected] staging -> staging (non-fast-forward)
$ git push --force origin staging
-> Forced update successful. Replaced 14 commits with rebased SHAs.
scenarios.riskSummary: Force-pushing a rebased branch to a shared environment where 5 other engineers are actively collaborating.
scenarios.question: Why does the SRE engineering doctrine strictly prohibit git push --force on shared branches?

options.label: It breaks Git servers permanently and requires reinstalling git on GitHub.
options.explanation: GitHub handles force-pushes natively, but downstream developers' local repositories will suffer divergent history conflicts.

options.label: Rebasing recalculates commit hashes; force-pushing overwrites the remote graph, causing colleagues' local branches to diverge and risking silent code loss.
options.explanation: Correct! Rewriting published history forces collaborators to reconcile divergent DAG histories. Work based on overwritten commits can be silently lost during careless merges.

options.label: Force-pushing converts all text files to binary blobs.
options.explanation: Force-push only moves remote reference pointers; it does not change file serialization.
